justification: SPECIFIC ITEM 1 (naive/pruned construction claim): read both SolveNaive and SolvePruned line by line. They take the same row parameter, the same usedCol array and the same 'for c in 0..n, skip if usedCol[c], else choose/recurse/un-choose' loop shape; SolvePruned's only structural addition is usedDiagUp/usedDiagDown and an extra continue condition inside the same loop. Because both recursions build the same column-assignment prefix in the same order (row 0 first, columns tried 0..n-1), a given (row, column-prefix) node is labeled identically in both trees. SolvePruned's condition (usedCol[c] || usedDiagUp[up] || usedDiagDown[down]) is a strict superset of SolveNaive's condition (usedCol[c] only) for deciding when to skip a child without recursing, so every child SolvePruned enters is a child SolveNaive would also enter, and SolvePruned can additionally skip children SolveNaive would still enter. That makes prunedNodes <= naiveNodes true by construction, not by luck of these particular measurements -- I verified this is actually true of the code, not merely asserted by the article's prose, and the article's own 'What these numbers do and don't prove' section states this argument explicitly and correctly (continue contributes zero nodes; recursing contributes >=1). The 'bounded by the same closed-form ceiling' follow-on claim is a direct corollary (pruned tree subset of naive tree subset of nothing larger) and is correctly hedged as an order-of-growth statement (order n!), not a claim about the solution count or about lowering the worst-case bound. SPECIFIC ITEM 2 (numbers): node counts n=4/6/8/10 naive (65, 1957, 109601, 9864101) exactly match OEIS A000522 (total arrangements / sum of partial permutations), which is independent, external confirmation the n=8 naive count of 109601 is the textbook-correct value for this exact search shape (one queen per row, column-uniqueness enforced, diagonal checked only at the leaf), not a fabricated or approximate figure. I additionally reimplemented every counting program in this article from scratch in Node.js (not reusing or transcribing the article's C#) and reproduced every reported number exactly: n=4/6/8/10 naive/pruned (65/17, 1957/153, 109601/2057, 9864101/35539), the buggy n=5 single-diagonal solver (23 accepted, 13 actually unsafe), the fixed n=5 solver (10 solutions, matching the well-known count), and the 4x4 Sudoku pair (naive 87381, pruned 11, both agreeing on 1 solution). The ratio table's percentages (26.15%, 7.82%, 1.88%, 0.36%) are correct arithmetic on those counts (17/65, 153/1957, 2057/109601, 35539/9864101), and the article's separately-stated 'about 1.9%' for n=8 is consistent rounding of the same 1.88% figure. The 4x4 naive count's closed form (4^0+...+4^8=87381) is exact arithmetic, independently confirmed. `node tools/run-code.mjs` also independently confirms all of this by actually compiling and running the article's own C# and diffing against its output blocks -- I ran it myself rather than trusting the article's claim of a passing run. SPECIFIC ITEM 3 (Sudoku NP-completeness restraint): grepped the full article text for 'NP-complet' and 'polynomial' (case-insensitive) -- zero matches. The Sedgewick & Wayne citation is used only for the general 'brute force on a large state space is infeasible' point (the N!-blowup argument I confirmed is actually on that page), explicitly scoped with 'for exhaustive search generally', never applied to claim a complexity-class result about Sudoku specifically. The restraint held. SPECIFIC ITEM 4 (C# array zero-init citation): fetched the live spec page. Section 17.3 Array creation states verbatim: 'Elements of arrays created by array_creation_expressions are always initialized to their default value ([section 9.3]).' The article's paraphrase ('the C# language specification guarantees that elements of an array created by new are always initialized to their type's default value') is an accurate, appropriately-unquoted paraphrase of that exact sentence, correctly anchored to #173-array-creation, and the claim that bool's default is false is standard/uncontroversial. Accurate. OTHER CHECKS: the intro's column-permutations example (6 permutations of 3 columns, lexicographic order) matches actual C# semantics and the run-code output. The Figure 1 diagram's attacked/safe labels for row1 c1/c2/c3 given row0 c0 are geometrically correct (|colDiff|==rowDiff only for c1). IsDiagonallySafe's single abs()-based check correctly catches both diagonal directions in one comparison (standard and correct), which is why the incremental pruned version needs two separate direction arrays instead of one. DEPTH: the article's closing section explicitly and correctly distinguishes 'pruning helps a lot empirically, on these measured inputs' from 'pruning lowers the worst-case asymptotic bound' -- a distinction most existing backtracking tutorials (GeeksforGeeks-style treatments in particular) do not make and often blur. That is a genuine depth advantage over typical existing coverage of this topic. The one thing keeping this short of a 10: the Knuth TAOCP citation (see issue below) attributes a specific formal characterization to a source page that, on inspection, does not itself contain that characterization.

issues.location: "Choose, explore, un-choose" section, first paragraph: "[Donald Knuth's characterization of backtrack programming](https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html), in The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 4, Fascicle 5, is the same idea stated formally: search a state space depth-first, and whenever a partial choice cannot possibly extend to a solution, abandon that branch rather than continuing to build on it."
issues.problem: I fetched the cited URL. It is Knuth's own TAOCP listing/bibliography page: it confirms Fascicle 5's title includes 'Introduction to Backtracking' (so the fascicle does exist and does cover this topic), but the page itself contains no definition or characterization of backtracking -- it is a table of contents/ordering page, not the fascicle's text. The article presents a specific formal paraphrase ('search a state space depth-first, and whenever a partial choice cannot possibly extend to a solution, abandon that branch...') as being Knuth's own characterization 'stated formally' in that source, but the cited page does not support that specific formal wording -- only that Knuth wrote a fascicle on the topic. This is the well-known, uncontroversial characterization of backtracking generally, so the underlying CS content is not wrong, but the citation attaches a specific claim ('is the same idea stated formally') to a page that cannot verify it, which is the kind of citation-support gap the brief's pilot-round lesson ('make sure that page supports that clause') flags.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either soften the sentence to attribute the characterization to backtracking generally rather than to a specific formal statement in the fascicle (e.g. "...is a formal version of the same idea, standard since Knuth's treatment in..."), or cite a source that actually contains Knuth's stated definition (e.g. a preprint/PDF of the fascicle's introduction, if one is publicly readable) instead of the bibliography page.
